name: Dhudhuroa
confidence_why: Blake and Reid 2002, the only linguistic description of this sleeping language, say outright that the historical records (Mathews 1909) are too thin to establish where stress fell, and Clark 2009 adds nothing beyond quoting them, so 'undetermined' is the faithful record but rests on a single source.
catalog_citation: Blake, Barry J. & Julie Reid. 2002. The Dhudhuroa language of northeastern Victoria: a description based on historical sources. Aboriginal History 26: 177-210. ANU Press open-access PDF.
catalog_locator: sec. 2 (Phonology), subsection 'Stress' (last paragraph before sec. 3 Morpho-syntax); also sec. 1 p.179 remark on Theddora, and the word-list preamble note on …
catalog_quote: Stress In the vast majority of Australian languages stress falls on the first syllable, but we cannot assume that this is always the case. Hercus reports stress on various syllables in Mathi-Mathi. Mathews marks stress on some words, mainly on a non-initial syllable, and mainly on the vowel a. There is not enough information for us to be able to say much about stress, and we must bear in mind that Mathews may have been hearing the relative sonority of the open vowel a over the close vowels as evidence of non-initial stress. ... [word-list preamble:] Stress is indicated by an accent (apostrophe) following the stressed syllable as in Mathews' published vocabulary.

audit.reasoning: The classification 'undetermined' rests on the only modern linguistic description of this sleeping language (Blake & Reid 2002, grammar sketch from historical sources), which we hold as the publisher's open-access PDF; the deciding passage is verbatim at printed p.186 and the word-list note at p.196. The authors explicitly say there is not enough information to say much about stress and flag Mathews' non-initial accents as possibly sonority-driven, so 'undetermined' is the faithful coding. The underlying primary publication (Mathews 1909) is also held and shows only sporadic accent marks with no rule. Glottolog has one descriptive reference in total; web checks (Wikipedia bibliography, VACL page, Clark 2009) surfaced nothing further on phonology. sources.citation: Mathews, R. H. 1909. The Dhudhuroa language of Victoria. American Anthropologist n.s. 11(2): 278-284.
sources.note: No statement on tone, pitch, accent or stress anywhere; the paper has no phonetic/orthographic paragraph and goes from the tribal introduction straight into 'Dhudhuroa Grammar' (articles, nouns, adjectives, pronouns, verbs, etc.) and a c.235-item vocabulary (pp. 281-284). sources.note: The only primary data; Blake & Reid report Mathews' accent marks fall mainly on non-initial syllables with a. A direct tally of accent placement in the ms (vs the published 1909 list we hold) is the only conceivable way to move this record off 'undetermined', and even then Blake & Reid's sonority caveat would stand.
